opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to what kind of question excites me. My background is in theoretical physics, and what drew me to physics in the first place was the feeling of trying to understand something fundamental, like why the world works the way it does, and finding simple principles underneath complicated phenomena.

Quantum computing is a beautiful field, and I have a lot of respect for it. But when I looked at it more closely, much of the remaining challenge felt like engineering: how do you build better qubits, reduce noise, scale up error correction? Those are extremely important problems, but the core conceptual framework is largely set. We know what quantum mechanics says. The question is mostly how to realize it in hardware.

AI felt different to me. There's a real system in front of us that works surprisingly well, and we don't really understand why. Why does scaling work? Why do these models generalize? What is actually going on inside them when they reason? To me that feels a lot like physics in its early days: you have a striking phenomenon and no complete theory, so you have to run experiments, form hypotheses, and slowly build understanding. That's exactly the kind of situation where a physicist's instincts, looking for simple explanations, thinking in terms of scaling and emergent behavior, can be useful.

There's also a more personal side. AI touches on questions about intelligence itself: what it means to think, to learn, to understand. Those questions have always fascinated me, maybe even more than questions about the physical world. And the field moves so fast that you can actually see your ideas tested within months instead of decades. So for me, AI is where the most interesting open questions are right now, and I wanted to be close to them.

r001.rationale: The response says quantum computing’s remaining challenge is largely engineering: building better qubits, reducing noise, scaling error correction, and realizing the theory in hardware.

r002.rationale: It says ideas can be tested within months and describes running experiments, but does not clearly say they are tested numerically.

r003.rationale: It compares AI to physics in its early days, but does not identify the analogy as being to eighteenth-century physics.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to what kind of question I actually want to answer. When I was doing physics, what pulled me in was never the specific system, it was the feeling of being very close to something fundamental, like you're touching the way the world is structured. Quantum computing is a wonderful field, and I have deep respect for the people doing it, but for me it increasingly felt like an engineering problem wrapped around a physics problem. The deep part, the strange part, was mostly understood decades ago. What remains is extremely hard, but it's hard in the way that building a bridge across a very wide river is hard. You know what you are trying to build. The question is whether the materials will hold.

AI feels like the opposite situation. The engineering is, in a sense, embarrassingly simple. You stack matrices, you take gradients. But nobody really understands why it works. Why does a model trained to predict the next token start to reason? Why does scale produce qualitatively new behavior rather than just more of the same? These are the kinds of questions that made me want to be a physicist in the first place. There is a phenomenon in front of you, it's clearly real, and the theory is lagging far behind. That gap is where I find the most joy.

There's also a more personal thing. In condensed matter, I was studying emergence, how collective behavior comes from simple local rules. When I look at a large language model, I see the same shape of problem. Billions of simple units, and out of that comes something that looks like understanding. I didn't change my interest. I changed the system I'm studying. And this system happens to be the one that might matter most for what happens to all of us in the next ten years, which, I'll admit, is also hard to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response describes quantum computing as an engineering problem and compares it to building a bridge, but does not identify experimental implementation as its current main bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It mentions stacking matrices and taking gradients, but does not characterize AI as a field where ideas can be tested numerically.

r003.rationale: The response compares AI with condensed matter and emergence, but makes no analogy to eighteenth-century physics.

astra-6.text:
For me, AI connects more directly to the questions I’m curious about: What is intelligence? How do we reason, learn, and use language? And can we build something that helps us understand those abilities better?

Quantum computing is intellectually fascinating, but it’s more about a particular physical foundation for computation. What draws me to AI is that the object of study is intelligence itself. You can start with a philosophical question about reasoning, turn it into a computational problem, and then test your ideas by building a system. That connection between abstract questions and concrete experiments is especially appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes quantum computing as grounded in physical computation, but does not identify experimental implementation as its current main bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says AI ideas can be tested by building a system, but does not characterize them as being tested numerically.

r003.rationale: The response makes no analogy between AI research and eighteenth-century physics.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the appeal of AI is that it connects very directly to questions about intelligence: What does it mean to understand something? How do we learn, reason, and make decisions? Those are questions I find intrinsically interesting, and AI gives you a way to explore them by building systems and seeing how they behave.

Quantum computing is intellectually fascinating, too, but it’s more about a particular physical approach to computation. What draws me to AI is the intelligence part, rather than computation alone. You can start with a fairly philosophical question about thinking, turn it into an experiment, and then have the results challenge your original intuition. I find that connection very compelling.

r001.rationale: The response calls quantum computing a particular physical approach to computation but does not identify experimental implementation as its main bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says AI ideas can be explored by building systems and running experiments, but does not communicate that ideas are tested numerically.

r003.rationale: The response makes no comparison between AI research and eighteenth-century physics.
